Thirty-two small episodes. One ceramic town.

NHK’s Blue Flowers and the Ceramic Forest begins tonight. Its romance is fictional; the argument over shape, painting and the future of Hasami ware is rooted in a real 400-year-old industry.

By Yuji Shimizu · YUJI @ Japan
Published October 26, 2026 at 13:45 JST · 6 min read

At 10:45 tonight, a fifteen-minute television slot will open on a bowl. Not a ceremonial masterpiece behind glass, but an object being formed, painted, argued over and prepared for someone’s table.

NHK’s new late-night drama Ao no Hana, Utsuwa no Mori—literally “Blue Flowers, Forest of Vessels”—starts on October 26 and runs Monday through Thursday for 32 episodes across eight weeks. The story follows Aoko, a painter at a pottery in Hasami, Nagasaki Prefecture, and Tatsuki, a ceramic artist returning from Finland who initially insists his forms need no painted decoration.

15 mineach Monday–Thursday broadcast
10 vols.completed manga by Yuki Kodama

The disagreement sounds like a romance mechanism: two skilled adults collide, then must work together for a spring event. But it also stages a real creative question. Is a vessel complete in its shape, or does the painted surface make it speak?

The town is not decorative scenery. Hasami built its identity on division of labor—forming, firing, glazing and painting moving through specialized hands. A story about two people learning to collaborate is also a story about how the industry itself works.

A manga becomes a nightly object

The drama adapts Yuki Kodama’s completed ten-volume manga, published by Shogakukan through Monthly Flowers. Kodama is also known for Kids on the Slope, another work where place, craft and the slow movement of adult feeling matter as much as plot.

Rena Matsui plays Aoko Baba, the Hasami-born painter. Hayate Ichinose plays Tatsuki Aokawa, the Finland-returned ceramic artist. The supporting cast includes Naoko Nishida, Naoko Zaizen, Takahiro Miura, Sosuke Fujima, Tamae Ando and Kentaro Maeda. Yoko Izumisawa writes the television adaptation, Eihiro Fukagawa directs, and Motohiro Hata performs the theme song, “Fragments.”

The short Yoru Dora format changes the rhythm. Four fifteen-minute episodes per week can follow workbench gestures that a two-hour film might compress: wet clay changing under pressure, a brush ending a line, a kiln opening after heat has made the result irreversible.

Official NHK trailer published October 16, 2026. It shows the actual cast, Hasami setting and ceramic work featured in the drama.

Why Hasami is different from the name on the box

Hasami is an inland town in northern Nagasaki Prefecture, close to the Saga border. Its ceramics developed more than 400 years ago. During the Edo period, the area became a major producer of durable, affordable tableware rather than objects reserved only for elite display.

That history created one of the drama’s hidden tensions: for centuries, ceramics made around Hasami could circulate under broader regional names and distribution systems. In contemporary branding, “Hasami ware” has become internationally recognizable for clean shapes, practical stacking and modern color, but its older identity was tied to mass production and everyday use.

The word utsuwa means a vessel or container, but in Japanese design conversation it often carries more warmth than the English “dish.” It can refer to the bowl that frames food, the cup that meets a hand, and metaphorically to a person’s capacity. The title uses utsuwa in a story about craft and emotional room.

The forest is a production system

A visitor to Hasami can see brick chimneys, kilns and workshops clustered around the town. Nakaoyama preserves the visible geography of production, including remains of large climbing kilns. The Nagasaki tourism authority describes the town not simply as a shopping destination but as a place where the history and landscape of ceramics remain legible.

Modern Hasami ware is often praised overseas for minimalist design, yet the industry is not one designer working alone. Molds, clay bodies, firing schedules, glazes, transfers, hand painting and quality control can involve different specialists. A successful cup is a coordinated chain.

That makes the fictional conflict between form and decoration more interesting. Tatsuki’s refusal of painting elevates the sculptural body; Aoko’s profession insists that surface carries knowledge too. Neither position is trivial. Their forced partnership asks whether authorship can remain singular inside a collaborative manufacturing town.

What international viewers should notice

First, watch the hands. Japanese craft television often turns finished objects into lifestyle images, but the trailer foregrounds process: sketching, brushing, handling and looking. A tiny hesitation can matter because clay and pigment preserve decisions.

Second, watch how Finland enters the story. Nordic design and contemporary Japanese tableware are frequently placed together in global retail, sometimes reduced to a shared “minimal” aesthetic. A character returning from Finland allows the drama to test that easy comparison from inside a Japanese production community.

Third, listen for workplace language. Terms for glaze, firing, kiln, painting and vessels belong to specific contexts. A useful everyday word is utsuwa—器—pronounced “oo-tsu-wah.” Example: この器は波佐見焼です, “This vessel is Hasami ware.” Readers can practice Japanese vocabulary free, without signup, in the Japanese Training Lab, then learn while playing in DraMap for iOS.

Why tonight matters beyond a premiere

The first episode is a national television introduction to a real town and industry. That can bring visitors and sales, but it can also flatten working culture into a photogenic backdrop. The strongest adaptation will let economic pressure, division of labor, failed pieces and creative disagreement remain visible.

The romance offers an accessible door. The deeper story is whether two makers can see value in the part of the object the other controls. Thirty-two short episodes give the production time to make that answer rather than declare it.

For viewers outside Japan, the official NHK page and trailer are the reliable starting points. Broadcast and streaming availability can vary by territory; this article does not imply worldwide distribution where none has been announced.
